parts:
Hi,

I am using the code below to fit my model. But every time I am getting at least 4 - 5 R_hat values > 1.1. Also is there option to check the convergence of our model at each iteration?



J = nlevels(Data_test$cate_var)

K = length(X_vars)
zero_vec_X = rep(0, K)
one_vec_X = rep(1, K)

nm.Data <- list(y_var = as.numeric(Data_test$y_var),
                Data_X = as.matrix(Data_test[, X_vars]),
                cate_var = as.numeric(Data_test$cate_var),
                S0 = diag(K) / (K + 2), 
                zero_vec_X = zero_vec_X,
                constraint_X_bound = matrix(rep(1,J*K),J,K)
)

nm.Constants <- list(N = nrow(Data_test),
                     K = K,
                     J = J
                     
)

######################### Parameters of Interest ################################################

nm.params <- c("alpha", "beta_X", "const")

######################### Initializations Function ##############################################

init_mu_X <- rtruncnorm(K, mean = 0, sd = 1, a = 0, b = 1)
init_Phi_X <- rwish((K+2), diag(K) * 0.01) 
init_beta_X <- rtmvnorm(J, mean = zero_vec_X, sigma = (diag(K) * 0.5), lower = zero_vec_X, upper = one_vec_X, algorithm = "gibbs")

nm.inits <- list("alpha" = rtruncnorm(nlevels(Data_test$cate_var), mean = 10, sd = 1, a = 0, b = 15), 
                 "mu_beta_X" = init_mu_X,
                 "Phi_X" = init_Phi_X,
                 "aux" = rgamma(1,1),
                 "beta_X" = init_beta_X
                 
)

nm.Dimensions <- list(zero_vec_X = c(K),
                      mu_beta_X = c(K),
                      beta_X = c(J, K),
                      Sigma_X = c(K, K),
                      Sigma2_X = c(K, K),
                      Phi_X = c(K, K),
                      Phi1_X = c(K, K),
                      Phi2_X = c(K, K)
)


############################ Define Model #####################################################

nm.Code <- nimbleCode({
  
  ####################
  # Specify Likelihood
  ####################
  for (n in 1:N) {
    
    y_var[n] ~ dnorm ((alpha[cate_var[n]] + inprod(beta_X[cate_var[n], ] , Data_X[n, ])), tau)

  }
  
  for (j in 1:J) {
    for (m in 1:K) {
      constraint_X_bound[j,m] ~ dconstraint(0 < beta_X[j,m] & beta_X[j,m] <= 1)
    }
  }
  
  ################
  # Specify Priors
  ################
  
  # X_vars Priors
  
  for (j in 1:J) {
    
    beta_X[j, 1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=mu_beta_X[], cov=Sigma_X[,]) 
    
    
    alpha[j] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  }
  
  # Error Prior
  aux ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)
  tau <- 1/aux
  
  ######################
  # Specify Hyper-Priors
  ######################
  Phi_X[1:K, 1:K] ~ dwish(S = S0[,], df = (K + 2)) #dinvwish(S = S0[,], df = (K+2))
  
  Sigma_X[1:K, 1:K] <- inverse(Phi_X[,])
  Sigma2_X[1:K, 1:K] <- Sigma_X[,]/0.01
  
  mu_beta_X[1:K] ~ dmnorm(zero_vec_X[], Sigma2_X[,])

  
})


############################# Build  model ############################################


set.seed(1234)
nm.Model <- nimbleModel(code=nm.Code, constants=nm.Constants, dimensions = nm.Dimensions,
                        data=nm.Data, inits=nm.inits, check = F, calculate = TRUE)

#pumpMCEM <- buildMCEM(model = nm.Model, latentNodes = c("aux", "Phi_X","mu_beta_X"), boxConstraints = list())

#pumpMLE <- pumpMCEM$run()

nm.Compiled <- compileNimble(nm.Model, showCompilerOutput = FALSE)
nm.Conf <- configureMCMC(nm.Model, print = TRUE)

nm.Conf$addMonitors(c("alpha", "beta_X"))

nm.MCMC <- buildMCMC(nm.Conf, enableWAIC = TRUE)

nm.ConfMCMC <- compileNimble(nm.MCMC, showCompilerOutput = F , project = nm.Model)

chains =2
nm.fit <- runMCMC(nm.ConfMCMC, niter = 100e3, nburnin = 30e3, inits = nm.inits, nchains = chains, 
                  setSeed = T, samples = T, summary = TRUE, WAIC = TRUE)


tmp <- nm.fit$summary$all.chains
nm.fit$WAIC



r_hat = NULL

for(i in rownames(tmp)){
  mcmc_samples <- NULL
  for(j in 1:chains){
    samples_chain <- nm.fit$`samples`[[j]]
    mcmc_samples <- cbind(mcmc_samples, samples_chain[, i])
  }
  colnames(mcmc_samples) <- names(nm.fit$`samples`)
  r_hat <- rbind(r_hat, cbind(i, R.hat(mcmc_samples)))
}
r_hat <- data.frame(r_hat)
names(r_hat) <- c("name", "R_hat")

r_hat$R_hat <- as.numeric(as.character(r_hat$R_hat))
length(which(r_hat$R_hat >= 1.1))

parts:
Hello bstat,

A few thoughts here:
 
 - it may be that the (0,1) constraint on the elements of dmnorm-distributed values slows mixing because a large number of constraints must all be 
simultaneously satisfied. To get a better sense, you might remove the constaints temporarily and see if mixing is much better so you know if that is the cause.
One possibility if you wanted to invest some time in this would be to remove the constraint and write your own user-defined sampler (documented in our manual)
 that implements the conjugate (i.e. Gibbs) update for beta_X but rejects any proposal that violates the constraint. That might work better than relying on NIMBLE's block samplers.

 - given that the model as written uses NIMBLE's Metropolis random walk block samplers, it's often the case that you need good initial values. You might 
also want to experiment with changing the initial proposal scale for these block samplers.

 - you might also try the AFSS sampler in place of the block samplers and see if that improves matters. See help(samplers) for more information

 - if you didn't have Phi_X involved in the prior for mu_beta_X as well as the prior for beta_X, then it should be assigned a conjugate sampler, which might mix better.
 For a parameter like mu_beta_X for which there is no replication, you may be best off assigning a fairly non-informative prior independently across the elements.
To get the conjugate sampler assigned, you might also have to directly use the precision matrix and avoid inverse(), which should also speed up computation.

 - and ultimately, you may just need to run the chain longer.

There is no way to assess mixing iteration by iteration. As documented in the manual, you can run the chain for a while, check the output, and then restart
the MCMC where it left off.

A couple other requests - please do include your name when mailing the list and do provide code that will run. Your code is missing dimensions for some of the variables ( as well as not providing
the data though we understand that might be confidential). 

Chris

On Wednesday, May 1, 2019 at 9:00:01 PM UTC-4, Chris Paciorek wrote:
Hello bstat,

A few thoughts here:
 
 - it may be that the (0,1) constraint on the elements of dmnorm-distributed values slows mixing because a large number of constraints must all be 
simultaneously satisfied. To get a better sense, you might remove the constaints temporarily and see if mixing is much better so you know if that is the cause.
One possibility if you wanted to invest some time in this would be to remove the constraint and write your own user-defined sampler (documented in our manual)
 that implements the conjugate (i.e. Gibbs) update for beta_X but rejects any proposal that violates the constraint. That might work better than relying on NIMBLE's block samplers.

 - given that the model as written uses NIMBLE's Metropolis random walk block samplers, it's often the case that you need good initial values. You might 
also want to experiment with changing the initial proposal scale for these block samplers.

 - you might also try the AFSS sampler in place of the block samplers and see if that improves matters. See help(samplers) for more information

 - if you didn't have Phi_X involved in the prior for mu_beta_X as well as the prior for beta_X, then it should be assigned a conjugate sampler, which might mix better.
 For a parameter like mu_beta_X for which there is no replication, you may be best off assigning a fairly non-informative prior independently across the elements.
To get the conjugate sampler assigned, you might also have to directly use the precision matrix and avoid inverse(), which should also speed up computation.

 - and ultimately, you may just need to run the chain longer.

There is no way to assess mixing iteration by iteration. As documented in the manual, you can run the chain for a while, check the output, and then restart
the MCMC where it left off.

A couple other requests - please do include your name when mailing the list and do provide code that will run. Your code is missing dimensions for some of the variables ( as well as not providing
the data though we understand that might be confidential). 

Chris

Hi Broti,

It doesn't make sense to use an "r" function in a nimble model.

If one has

x[i] ~ dnorm(mean, sd = sigma),

this is, in effect, converted to

logProb_x[i] <- dnorm(x[i], mean, sigma, log = TRUE)

MCMC needs to calculate "d" functions, not to simulate from "r" functions.  

One can simulate with a nimble model.  When one does so, nimble automatically uses the corresponding "r" function based on a name like "dnorm".

If the above declaration for x[i] is in a model, enclosed in for(i in 1:10), then

Rmodel$simulate('x[3]')

will, in effect, be converted to

x[3] <- rnorm(1, mean, sigma).

In both of your trials, the error message says the first argument to a "d" function should be  "x".  This is similar to all R density functions.  E.g. the first argument to dnorm is x.  The immediate problem in both of your trials is that you have made the first argument to both nimbleRcalls be "n".  Normally, "n" is the first argument to an "r" function but not a "d" function.

Please try something like 
dmultinorm <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(), mean = double(), sigma =  double(), lower = integer(0),
upper = integer(0)){}, Rfun = 'dtmvnorm',
returnType = double(), envir = .GlobalEnv)

with
demoCode <- nimbleCode({
   for(i in 1:4) {x[i] ~ dmultinorm(mean = 0, sigma = 1, lower = 0, upper = 1)} 
})

Also please read the user manual sections on nimbleRcall and on user-defined distributions.  I think those two sections provide the details you need.

On Monday, May 6, 2019 at 1:15:40 PM UTC-4, nimble.stats wrote:

Hi Broti,

It doesn't make sense to use an "r" function in a nimble model.

If one has

x[i] ~ dnorm(mean, sd = sigma),

this is, in effect, converted to

logProb_x[i] <- dnorm(x[i], mean, sigma, log = TRUE)

MCMC needs to calculate "d" functions, not to simulate from "r" functions.  

One can simulate with a nimble model.  When one does so, nimble automatically uses the corresponding "r" function based on a name like "dnorm".

If the above declaration for x[i] is in a model, enclosed in for(i in 1:10), then

Rmodel$simulate('x[3]')

will, in effect, be converted to

x[3] <- rnorm(1, mean, sigma).

In both of your trials, the error message says the first argument to a "d" function should be  "x".  This is similar to all R density functions.  E.g. the first argument to dnorm is x.  The immediate problem in both of your trials is that you have made the first argument to both nimbleRcalls be "n".  Normally, "n" is the first argument to an "r" function but not a "d" function.

Please try something like 
dmultinorm <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(), mean = double(), sigma =  double(), lower = integer(0),
                                 upper = integer(0)){}, Rfun = 'dtmvnorm', 
                                 returnType = double(), envir = .GlobalEnv)

with
demoCode <- nimbleCode({
   for(i in 1:4) {x[i] ~ dmultinorm(mean = 0, sigma = 1, lower = 0, upper = 1)} 
})

Also please read the user manual sections on nimbleRcall and on user-defined distributions.  I think those two sections provide the details you need.

On Wednesday, May 1, 2019 at 9:00:01 PM UTC-4, Chris Paciorek wrote:
Hello bstat,

A few thoughts here:
 
 - it may be that the (0,1) constraint on the elements of dmnorm-distributed values slows mixing because a large number of constraints must all be 
simultaneously satisfied. To get a better sense, you might remove the constaints temporarily and see if mixing is much better so you know if that is the cause.
One possibility if you wanted to invest some time in this would be to remove the constraint and write your own user-defined sampler (documented in our manual)
 that implements the conjugate (i.e. Gibbs) update for beta_X but rejects any proposal that violates the constraint. That might work better than relying on NIMBLE's block samplers.

 - given that the model as written uses NIMBLE's Metropolis random walk block samplers, it's often the case that you need good initial values. You might 
also want to experiment with changing the initial proposal scale for these block samplers.

 - you might also try the AFSS sampler in place of the block samplers and see if that improves matters. See help(samplers) for more information

 - if you didn't have Phi_X involved in the prior for mu_beta_X as well as the prior for beta_X, then it should be assigned a conjugate sampler, which might mix better.
 For a parameter like mu_beta_X for which there is no replication, you may be best off assigning a fairly non-informative prior independently across the elements.
To get the conjugate sampler assigned, you might also have to directly use the precision matrix and avoid inverse(), which should also speed up computation.

 - and ultimately, you may just need to run the chain longer.

There is no way to assess mixing iteration by iteration. As documented in the manual, you can run the chain for a while, check the output, and then restart
the MCMC where it left off.

A couple other requests - please do include your name when mailing the list and do provide code that will run. Your code is missing dimensions for some of the variables ( as well as not providing
the data though we understand that might be confidential). 

Chris

Hi Broti,

It doesn't make sense to use an "r" function in a nimble model.

If one has

x[i] ~ dnorm(mean, sd = sigma),

this is, in effect, converted to

logProb_x[i] <- dnorm(x[i], mean, sigma, log = TRUE)

MCMC needs to calculate "d" functions, not to simulate from "r" functions.  

One can simulate with a nimble model.  When one does so, nimble automatically uses the corresponding "r" function based on a name like "dnorm".

If the above declaration for x[i] is in a model, enclosed in for(i in 1:10), then

Rmodel$simulate('x[3]')

will, in effect, be converted to

x[3] <- rnorm(1, mean, sigma).

In both of your trials, the error message says the first argument to a "d" function should be  "x".  This is similar to all R density functions.  E.g. the first argument to dnorm is x.  The immediate problem in both of your trials is that you have made the first argument to both nimbleRcalls be "n".  Normally, "n" is the first argument to an "r" function but not a "d" function.

Please try something like 
dmultinorm <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(), mean = double(), sigma =  double(), lower = integer(0),
                                 upper = integer(0)){}, Rfun = 'dtmvnorm', 
                                 returnType = double(), envir = .GlobalEnv)

with
demoCode <- nimbleCode({
   for(i in 1:4) {x[i] ~ dmultinorm(mean = 0, sigma = 1, lower = 0, upper = 1)} 
})

Also please read the user manual sections on nimbleRcall and on user-defined distributions.  I think those two sections provide the details you need.

On Wednesday, May 1, 2019 at 9:00:01 PM UTC-4, Chris Paciorek wrote:
Hello bstat,

A few thoughts here:
 
 - it may be that the (0,1) constraint on the elements of dmnorm-distributed values slows mixing because a large number of constraints must all be 
simultaneously satisfied. To get a better sense, you might remove the constaints temporarily and see if mixing is much better so you know if that is the cause.
One possibility if you wanted to invest some time in this would be to remove the constraint and write your own user-defined sampler (documented in our manual)
 that implements the conjugate (i.e. Gibbs) update for beta_X but rejects any proposal that violates the constraint. That might work better than relying on NIMBLE's block samplers.

 - given that the model as written uses NIMBLE's Metropolis random walk block samplers, it's often the case that you need good initial values. You might 
also want to experiment with changing the initial proposal scale for these block samplers.

 - you might also try the AFSS sampler in place of the block samplers and see if that improves matters. See help(samplers) for more information

 - if you didn't have Phi_X involved in the prior for mu_beta_X as well as the prior for beta_X, then it should be assigned a conjugate sampler, which might mix better.
 For a parameter like mu_beta_X for which there is no replication, you may be best off assigning a fairly non-informative prior independently across the elements.
To get the conjugate sampler assigned, you might also have to directly use the precision matrix and avoid inverse(), which should also speed up computation.

 - and ultimately, you may just need to run the chain longer.

There is no way to assess mixing iteration by iteration. As documented in the manual, you can run the chain for a while, check the output, and then restart
the MCMC where it left off.

A couple other requests - please do include your name when mailing the list and do provide code that will run. Your code is missing dimensions for some of the variables ( as well as not providing
the data though we understand that might be confidential). 

Chris

Hi Broti,

It doesn't make sense to use an "r" function in a nimble model.

If one has

x[i] ~ dnorm(mean, sd = sigma),

this is, in effect, converted to

logProb_x[i] <- dnorm(x[i], mean, sigma, log = TRUE)

MCMC needs to calculate "d" functions, not to simulate from "r" functions.  

One can simulate with a nimble model.  When one does so, nimble automatically uses the corresponding "r" function based on a name like "dnorm".

If the above declaration for x[i] is in a model, enclosed in for(i in 1:10), then

Rmodel$simulate('x[3]')

will, in effect, be converted to

x[3] <- rnorm(1, mean, sigma).

In both of your trials, the error message says the first argument to a "d" function should be  "x".  This is similar to all R density functions.  E.g. the first argument to dnorm is x.  The immediate problem in both of your trials is that you have made the first argument to both nimbleRcalls be "n".  Normally, "n" is the first argument to an "r" function but not a "d" function.

Please try something like 
dmultinorm <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(), mean = double(), sigma =  double(), lower = integer(0),
                                 upper = integer(0)){}, Rfun = 'dtmvnorm', 
                                 returnType = double(), envir = .GlobalEnv)

demoCode <- nimbleCode({
   for(i in 1:4) {x[i] ~ dmultinorm(mean = 0, sigma = 1, lower = 0, upper = 1)} 
})

Hello bstat,

A few thoughts here:
 
 - it may be that the (0,1) constraint on the elements of dmnorm-distributed values slows mixing because a large number of constraints must all be 
simultaneously satisfied. To get a better sense, you might remove the constaints temporarily and see if mixing is much better so you know if that is the cause.
One possibility if you wanted to invest some time in this would be to remove the constraint and write your own user-defined sampler (documented in our manual)
 that implements the conjugate (i.e. Gibbs) update for beta_X but rejects any proposal that violates the constraint. That might work better than relying on NIMBLE's block samplers.

 - given that the model as written uses NIMBLE's Metropolis random walk block samplers, it's often the case that you need good initial values. You might 
also want to experiment with changing the initial proposal scale for these block samplers.

 - you might also try the AFSS sampler in place of the block samplers and see if that improves matters. See help(samplers) for more information

 - if you didn't have Phi_X involved in the prior for mu_beta_X as well as the prior for beta_X, then it should be assigned a conjugate sampler, which might mix better.
 For a parameter like mu_beta_X for which there is no replication, you may be best off assigning a fairly non-informative prior independently across the elements.
To get the conjugate sampler assigned, you might also have to directly use the precision matrix and avoid inverse(), which should also speed up computation.

 - and ultimately, you may just need to run the chain longer.

There is no way to assess mixing iteration by iteration. As documented in the manual, you can run the chain for a while, check the output, and then restart
the MCMC where it left off.

Hi Broti,

It doesn't make sense to use an "r" function in a nimble model.

If one has

x[i] ~ dnorm(mean, sd = sigma),

this is, in effect, converted to

logProb_x[i] <- dnorm(x[i], mean, sigma, log = TRUE)

MCMC needs to calculate "d" functions, not to simulate from "r" functions.  

One can simulate with a nimble model.  When one does so, nimble automatically uses the corresponding "r" function based on a name like "dnorm".

If the above declaration for x[i] is in a model, enclosed in for(i in 1:10), then

Rmodel$simulate('x[3]')

will, in effect, be converted to

x[3] <- rnorm(1, mean, sigma).

In both of your trials, the error message says the first argument to a "d" function should be  "x".  This is similar to all R density functions.  E.g. the first argument to dnorm is x.  The immediate problem in both of your trials is that you have made the first argument to both nimbleRcalls be "n".  Normally, "n" is the first argument to an "r" function but not a "d" function.

Please try something like 
dmultinorm <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(), mean = double(), sigma =  double(), lower = integer(0),
                                 upper = integer(0)){}, Rfun = 'dtmvnorm', 
                                 returnType = double(), envir = .GlobalEnv)

with
demoCode <- nimbleCode({
   for(i in 1:4) {x[i] ~ dmultinorm(mean = 0, sigma = 1, lower = 0, upper = 1)} 
})

Also please read the user manual sections on nimbleRcall and on user-defined distributions.  I think those two sections provide the details you need.

On Wednesday, May 1, 2019 at 9:00:01 PM UTC-4, Chris Paciorek wrote:
Hello bstat,

A few thoughts here:
 
 - it may be that the (0,1) constraint on the elements of dmnorm-distributed values slows mixing because a large number of constraints must all be 
simultaneously satisfied. To get a better sense, you might remove the constaints temporarily and see if mixing is much better so you know if that is the cause.
One possibility if you wanted to invest some time in this would be to remove the constraint and write your own user-defined sampler (documented in our manual)
 that implements the conjugate (i.e. Gibbs) update for beta_X but rejects any proposal that violates the constraint. That might work better than relying on NIMBLE's block samplers.

 - given that the model as written uses NIMBLE's Metropolis random walk block samplers, it's often the case that you need good initial values. You might 
also want to experiment with changing the initial proposal scale for these block samplers.

 - you might also try the AFSS sampler in place of the block samplers and see if that improves matters. See help(samplers) for more information

 - if you didn't have Phi_X involved in the prior for mu_beta_X as well as the prior for beta_X, then it should be assigned a conjugate sampler, which might mix better.
 For a parameter like mu_beta_X for which there is no replication, you may be best off assigning a fairly non-informative prior independently across the elements.
To get the conjugate sampler assigned, you might also have to directly use the precision matrix and avoid inverse(), which should also speed up computation.

 - and ultimately, you may just need to run the chain longer.

There is no way to assess mixing iteration by iteration. As documented in the manual, you can run the chain for a while, check the output, and then restart
the MCMC where it left off.

A couple other requests - please do include your name when mailing the list and do provide code that will run. Your code is missing dimensions for some of the variables ( as well as not providing
the data though we understand that might be confidential). 

Chris

Hi Broti,

It doesn't make sense to use an "r" function in a nimble model.

If one has

x[i] ~ dnorm(mean, sd = sigma),

this is, in effect, converted to

logProb_x[i] <- dnorm(x[i], mean, sigma, log = TRUE)

MCMC needs to calculate "d" functions, not to simulate from "r" functions.  

One can simulate with a nimble model.  When one does so, nimble automatically uses the corresponding "r" function based on a name like "dnorm".

If the above declaration for x[i] is in a model, enclosed in for(i in 1:10), then

Rmodel$simulate('x[3]')

will, in effect, be converted to

x[3] <- rnorm(1, mean, sigma).

In both of your trials, the error message says the first argument to a "d" function should be  "x".  This is similar to all R density functions.  E.g. the first argument to dnorm is x.  The immediate problem in both of your trials is that you have made the first argument to both nimbleRcalls be "n".  Normally, "n" is the first argument to an "r" function but not a "d" function.

Please try something like 
dmultinorm <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(), mean = double(), sigma =  double(), lower = integer(0),
                                 upper = integer(0)){}, Rfun = 'dtmvnorm', 
                                 returnType = double(), envir = .GlobalEnv)

with
demoCode <- nimbleCode({
   for(i in 1:4) {x[i] ~ dmultinorm(mean = 0, sigma = 1, lower = 0, upper = 1)} 
})

Also please read the user manual sections on nimbleRcall and on user-defined distributions.  I think those two sections provide the details you need.

On Wednesday, May 1, 2019 at 9:00:01 PM UTC-4, Chris Paciorek wrote:
Hello bstat,

A few thoughts here:
 
 - it may be that the (0,1) constraint on the elements of dmnorm-distributed values slows mixing because a large number of constraints must all be 
simultaneously satisfied. To get a better sense, you might remove the constaints temporarily and see if mixing is much better so you know if that is the cause.
One possibility if you wanted to invest some time in this would be to remove the constraint and write your own user-defined sampler (documented in our manual)
 that implements the conjugate (i.e. Gibbs) update for beta_X but rejects any proposal that violates the constraint. That might work better than relying on NIMBLE's block samplers.

 - given that the model as written uses NIMBLE's Metropolis random walk block samplers, it's often the case that you need good initial values. You might 
also want to experiment with changing the initial proposal scale for these block samplers.

 - you might also try the AFSS sampler in place of the block samplers and see if that improves matters. See help(samplers) for more information

 - if you didn't have Phi_X involved in the prior for mu_beta_X as well as the prior for beta_X, then it should be assigned a conjugate sampler, which might mix better.
 For a parameter like mu_beta_X for which there is no replication, you may be best off assigning a fairly non-informative prior independently across the elements.
To get the conjugate sampler assigned, you might also have to directly use the precision matrix and avoid inverse(), which should also speed up computation.

 - and ultimately, you may just need to run the chain longer.

There is no way to assess mixing iteration by iteration. As documented in the manual, you can run the chain for a while, check the output, and then restart
the MCMC where it left off.

the data though we understand that might be confidential).
